title: Coding strand with bases before the start codon and a stop codon
description: Rows of base boxes for a 24-base DNA coding strand 5′ GCCA ATG GTT CAC TGG AAA TAA GC 3′, its template strand, the mRNA, the tRNA anticodons and the amino acids, with brackets under each codon of the mRNA from AUG to the stop codon UAA: Met, Val, His, Trp and Lys as a chain of beads, then Stop, and no amino acids under the four bases before AUG or the two after UAA
caption: A DNA coding strand with four bases before the start codon. Translation starts at the first AUG in the mRNA, so the bases before it get no codons or amino acids, and a bracket marks each codon read after it. It ends at the stop codon UAA, which codes for no amino acid and has no tRNA, so the chain is Met, Val, His, Trp and Lys, and the last two bases are not read.

title: Codon chart: the standard genetic code table
description: A square codon chart with the first base U, C, A, G down the left, the second base across the top and the third base down the right, each of the 16 cells listing four codons with their amino acids, AUG Met (Start) and the stop codons UAA, UAG and UGA in bold on gray
caption: The standard genetic code as a square table. Find a codon’s first base down the left, its second across the top and its third down the right of the cell. Each of the 64 codons is listed with the amino acid it codes for in three-letter code; AUG, methionine, is the start codon, and UAA, UAG and UGA are the stop codons.

title: DNA complementary strand worksheet: draw the other half
description: A DNA coding strand 5′ ATG CGT ACC TTA GGC ATA 3′ in boxes, with a row of 18 empty boxes under it labeled DNA template strand, running 3′ to 5′, for students to write the complementary bases in
caption: Half a DNA molecule for students to complete: the coding strand is written in, 5′ to 3′, and the template strand under it is left as empty boxes. Students pair each base, A with T and G with C, and see from the 5′ and 3′ labels that the two strands run in opposite directions. The answer key gives the template strand, 3′-TAC GCA TGG AAT CCG TAT-5′.

title: Transcription multiple choice: spot the wrong base pairing in the mRNA
description: Answer choice B: the DNA coding strand 5′ ATG CCT AAG TTC GGC 3′, the template strand 3′ TAC GGA TTC AAG CCG 5′ and an mRNA row 5′ AUG CCU CAG UUC GGC 3′, where the seventh base, C, does not pair with the T above it
caption: One answer choice for a transcription question: two DNA strands and the mRNA made from the template strand, with one base deliberately wrong. The seventh mRNA base is C, where the template strand’s T calls for A. Make the other choices with no mistakes or with a different set shuffled, and print each with its letter as the title.

title: Transcription and translation from a template strand starting TAC
description: Five rows of base boxes lined up base under base, each with its 5′ and 3′ ends: the DNA coding strand 5′ ATG CCT AAG TTC GGC 3′, the DNA template strand 3′ TAC GGA TTC AAG CCG 5′, the mRNA 5′ AUG CCU AAG UUC GGC 3′, the tRNA anticodons UAC GGA UUC AAG CCG, and a chain of amino acid beads Met, Pro, Lys, Phe and Gly, one under each codon
caption: A gene transcribed and translated, every row lined up base under base. The DNA template strand, written 3′ to 5′, starts TAC; the coding strand above it pairs A with T and G with C, and the mRNA below matches the coding strand with U in place of T. Each tRNA anticodon is complementary to its mRNA codon, and the amino acids methionine, proline, lysine, phenylalanine and glycine are joined in a chain under their codons.

title: Competitive and non-competitive inhibitor graph (rate against substrate concentration)
description: Graph of rate of reaction against substrate concentration with no numbers on the axes: three curves rising and levelling off, no inhibitor (solid blue), a competitive inhibitor (dashed red) reaching the same Vmax more slowly, and a non-competitive inhibitor (dotted green) levelling off at a lower Vmax, with dashed Vmax lines labeled Vmax and Vmax (non-competitive) at the y-axis and a key under the graph
caption: The rate of reaction against substrate concentration for an enzyme on its own (solid blue), with a competitive inhibitor (dashed red) and with a non-competitive inhibitor (dotted green), drawn as Michaelis–Menten curves. With a competitive inhibitor the rate climbs more slowly but reaches the same Vmax, since enough substrate outcompetes it; with a non-competitive inhibitor it levels off at a lower Vmax. Dashed lines across mark each Vmax, labeled at the y-axis: the enzyme’s own, which the competitive inhibitor shares, and the non-competitive inhibitor’s.

title: Enzyme activity against pH: pepsin, amylase and trypsin
description: Graph of rate of reaction against pH with no numbers on the axes: three bell-shaped curves, pepsin (solid blue) peaking at pH 2, salivary amylase (dashed red) at pH 7 and trypsin (dotted green) at pH 8, each peak marked with a dot, a dashed line down to the pH axis and the label Optimum, and a key under the graph
caption: The rate of reaction against pH for three digestive enzymes, drawn as shapes with no numbers on the axes. Pepsin (solid blue) works best at about pH 2, as in the stomach, salivary amylase (dashed red) at about pH 7, as in the mouth, and trypsin (dotted green) at about pH 8, as in the small intestine. Each curve is a bell around its optimum, marked with a dot and a dashed line down to the pH axis, and falls to zero either side where the enzyme denatures.

title: Enzyme activity against temperature: human enzyme and Taq polymerase
description: Graph of rate of reaction against temperature (°C) with no numbers on the axes: a solid blue curve for a human enzyme and a dashed red curve for Taq polymerase, each rising slowly to an optimum marked with a dot and a dashed line, labeled Optimum, then falling steeply to a dot on the axis labeled Denatured
caption: The rate of reaction against temperature for an enzyme from the human body (solid blue) and Taq polymerase, from bacteria living in hot springs (dashed red). Each rate rises gently as the temperature goes up, peaks at the enzyme’s optimum, about 37 °C for the human enzyme and 75 °C for Taq polymerase, then falls steeply as the enzyme denatures. Dots mark each optimum, with a dashed line down to the temperature axis, and where each curve falls to zero.

title: Enzyme and temperature graph worksheet: label the optimum and denaturation
description: Black and white graph of rate of reaction against temperature (°C) with no numbers on the axes: one curve rising to a peak and falling steeply to the axis, a dot on the peak with a dashed line down and a dot where the curve meets the axis, each with a blank line for students to label
caption: A worksheet graph of a human enzyme’s rate of reaction against temperature, in black and white with no numbers on the axes. The rate rises to a peak and then falls steeply to zero. A dot marks the peak, with a dashed line down to the temperature axis, and another marks where the rate reaches zero, each with a blank line for students to write what happens there.

title: Michaelis–Menten graph with Vmax, ½Vmax and Km
description: Graph of rate of reaction against substrate concentration with no numbers on the axes: one curve rising steeply and levelling off under a dashed line labeled Vmax, with a dot at half that height joined by dashed lines to the y-axis, labeled ½Vmax, and down to the x-axis, labeled Km
caption: A Michaelis–Menten curve: the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction rises steeply as substrate is added, then levels off as every active site becomes busy. A dashed line across marks the top rate, Vmax. A dot marks where the rate is half of Vmax, with dashed lines across to the y-axis, labeled ½Vmax, and down to the substrate concentration that gives it, labeled Km.

title: DNA fingerprinting gel: crime scene and three suspects
description: A glowing agarose gel with five lanes labeled Ladder, Crime scene, Suspect 1, Suspect 2 and Suspect 3; the 1 kb ladder is labeled from 10,000 bp down to 500 bp, and each other lane has four bands
caption: A 1% agarose gel with glowing bands on a dark background, as a stained gel looks under UV light. The first lane is a 1 kb ladder with its sizes written beside it, from 10,000 bp to 500 bp; the next holds DNA from a crime scene, and the last three hold DNA from three suspects, four bands each. Students compare each suspect’s bands with the crime scene’s to decide which one matches.

title: Lambda DNA restriction digest gel with a ruler for a standard curve
description: A 0.8% agarose gel with four lanes labeled Ladder, Uncut, EcoRI and BamHI, the λ DNA / HindIII ladder labeled from 23.1 kb to 0.125 kb, and a centimeter ruler beside the gel from 0 to 8 cm
caption: A 0.8% agarose gel with a λ DNA / HindIII ladder in the first lane, labeled in kb from 23.1 kb to 0.125 kb, then uncut λ DNA and λ DNA cut with EcoRI and with BamHI. A ruler in cm and mm runs beside the gel, with 0 at the bottom of the wells, so students can measure how far each band ran and plot a standard curve from the ladder. The largest pieces crowd together near the wells, and in the EcoRI and BamHI lanes, fragments too close in size to separate on this gel run together as thicker bands.

title: Paternity test gel: mother, child and two possible fathers
description: A pale blue agarose gel with blue bands in five lanes labeled Ladder, Mother, Child, Father 1 and Father 2; the 1 kb ladder is labeled from 10,000 bp to 500 bp, and each other lane has four bands
caption: A 1% agarose gel in blue, as a classroom DNA stain leaves it, with a 1 kb ladder labeled from 10,000 bp to 500 bp in the first lane. The other lanes hold DNA from a mother, her child and two possible fathers, four bands each. Every band of the child’s must come from the mother or the father, so students match the child’s bands to decide which man is the father.

title: Plasmid restriction digest gel worksheet: draw the double digest
description: A 1% agarose gel with four lanes labeled Ladder, EcoRI, HindIII and Both; blank lines beside the ladder’s ten bands, empty circles at both ends for the electrodes, and the Both lane left empty
caption: A 1% agarose gel of a 5,000 bp plasmid cut by EcoRI, which leaves one band, by HindIII, which leaves two, and by both enzymes together. The Both lane is left empty for students to draw its bands from the two single digests. The 1 kb ladder’s ten bands have blank lines beside them for students to label, and the electrodes are empty circles for them to mark − and +.

title: PTC taster gene PCR and HaeIII digest gel with a 100 bp ladder
description: A 2% agarose gel with five numbered lanes labeled Ladder, Uncut, TT, Tt and tt; the 100 bp ladder is labeled from 1517 bp down to 100 bp, the uncut and tt lanes have one band, TT has two and Tt has three
caption: A 2% agarose gel with a 100 bp ladder in lane 1, labeled from 1517 bp to 100 bp, with its 500 and 517 bp bands run together as one. Lane 2 holds the uncut PCR product from the TAS2R38 bitter taste gene; lanes 3 to 5 hold it after cutting with HaeIII, which cuts the taster allele but not the nontaster allele, for a TT taster, a Tt taster and a tt nontaster. The smallest fragment is faint and runs past the 100 bp band, below what a 2% gel separates well.

title: Black and white P10 micropipette set to 4.6 µL
description: A black and white outline drawing of a 10 µL micropipette with no tip, its volume display reading 0, 4, 6 from top to bottom with a line above the 6
caption: A 10 µL micropipette (a P10) drawn in black outline with no tip, ready to photocopy. Its display reads 0, 4 and 6 from top to bottom. With no red ink, the line across the display above the 6 marks the decimal point, so the bottom digit is the tenths of a µL.

title: P1000 micropipette set to 820 µL
description: A 1000 µL micropipette with a wide shaft and a blue tip, its volume display reading 0, 8, 2, 0 from the top
caption: A 1000 µL micropipette (a P1000), the largest size, with a wide shaft, a blue tip and a blue plunger cap. Its display is read from the top, where the first digit counts thousands of µL: the 0 there shows it is set below 1000 µL, and the 8, 2 and 0 under it are the hundreds, tens and ones.

title: P2 micropipette set to 0.85 µL
description: A 2 µL micropipette with a slim shaft and a clear tip, its volume display reading 0, 8, 5 from top to bottom, the 8 and 5 in red below a line
caption: A 2 µL micropipette (a P2), the smallest size, with a slim shaft and a clear tip. Its display reads 0, 8 and 5 from top to bottom, with the 8 and 5 in red below a line: on a P2 the digits stand for ones, tenths and hundredths of a µL. The 0 on top means less than 1 µL, a common trip-up for students.

title: P20 micropipette set to 15.7 µL
description: A 20 µL micropipette with a yellow tip, its volume display reading 1, 5, 7 from top to bottom, the 7 in red below a line
caption: A 20 µL micropipette (a P20) with a yellow tip and its size printed above the volume display. The display reads 1, 5 and 7 from top to bottom, with the 7 in red below a line across the display. On a P20 the digits stand for tens, ones and tenths of a µL, so the red digit is the tenths.

title: P200 micropipette set to 154 µL
description: A 200 µL micropipette with a yellow tip, its volume display reading 1, 5, 4 from top to bottom, all in black
caption: A 200 µL micropipette (a P200) with a yellow tip and a yellow plunger cap. Its display reads 1, 5 and 4 from top to bottom, all in black: a P200’s digits stand for hundreds, tens and ones of a µL, so it has no red digits and no decimal line. It is set in whole microliters, from 20 to 200 µL.

title: AP Biology dialysis tubing bag with glucose and starch
description: A dialysis tubing bag tied to a rod, in a beaker of pure water, holding white glucose particles and a dark starch particle among blue water particles; water arrows point into the bag and a dashed arrow labeled glucose points out of it; then an arrow to the same bag swollen larger, with glucose particles now on both sides and the starch still inside
caption: A dialysis tubing bag holding 15% glucose and 3% starch, in a beaker of pure water. Glucose is small enough to cross the tubing, so it moves out of the bag until its concentration is the same on both sides; starch can’t cross, so the beaker is hypotonic to the bag and water moves in. On the right the bag has swollen, with glucose on both sides and the starch still inside.

title: Plant cell plasmolysis in a strong sugar solution
description: A plant cell with a nucleus and chloroplasts, its cell wall, vacuole and cell membrane labeled down the left, in a box crowded with gray sucrose particles, with water arrows pointing out across the wall, labeled Hypertonic solution, then an arrow to the same cell plasmolyzed, its membrane and cytoplasm pulled away from the wall into a rounded shape around a small vacuole, with the sugar solution filling the gap
caption: A plant cell, 5% sucrose in its vacuole, in a 30% sucrose solution. The solution is hypertonic, so water leaves the vacuole and the cytoplasm and crosses the membrane and the cell wall. On the right the cell is plasmolyzed: the vacuole has shrunk, the membrane and cytoplasm have pulled away from the wall, and the sugar solution, which passes through the wall, fills the gap between them.

title: Red blood cell in 0.9% saline: isotonic, no net movement
description: A red blood cell with gray NaCl particles inside in a box of 0.9% NaCl solution with as many particles per space, water arrows going both ways across the membrane labeled No net movement, labeled Isotonic solution, then an arrow to the same normal disc-shaped cell
caption: A red blood cell, 0.9% NaCl inside, in 0.9% saline, the concentration of normal saline drips. Inside and outside are isotonic, so water crosses the membrane equally both ways: no net movement. The cell keeps its normal biconcave shape, drawn pale in the middle.

title: Red blood cell in pure water: hypotonic, swells and bursts
description: A red blood cell with a few gray NaCl particles inside, in a box of pure water full of blue water particles, with water arrows pointing into the cell, labeled Hypotonic solution, then an arrow to the same cell swollen and burst open, its membrane torn, labeled Bursts (lysed)
caption: A red blood cell, 0.9% NaCl inside, put in pure water. The water outside is hypotonic to the cell, so water moves into it by osmosis, shown by the arrows. On the right the cell has swollen until its membrane tears and it bursts, called hemolysis or lysis.

title: Red blood cell in 5% salt solution: hypertonic, shrinks and crenates
description: A red blood cell with a few gray NaCl particles inside, in a box crowded with NaCl particles, with water arrows pointing out of the cell, labeled Hypertonic solution, then an arrow to the same cell shrunken with spiky edges, labeled Shrinks (crenated)
caption: A red blood cell, 0.9% NaCl inside, in a 5% NaCl solution. The solution is hypertonic to the cell, so water moves out of it by osmosis, shown by the arrows. On the right the cell has shrunk and its edge has crinkled into spikes: it is crenated.

title: Red blood cells in hypotonic, isotonic and hypertonic solutions
description: Three red blood cells, each in a box of salt solution with gray NaCl particles and blue water particles: A in a hypotonic 0.45% solution, swollen round, with water arrows pointing in; B in an isotonic 0.9% solution, a normal disc with arrows both ways and the words No net movement; C in a hypertonic 1.8% solution, shrunken with spiky edges, with water arrows pointing out
caption: The same red blood cell, 0.9% NaCl inside, in three salt solutions. In the hypotonic solution (0.45% NaCl) water moves in and the cell swells; in the isotonic solution (0.9%) water crosses equally both ways, so there is no net movement and it stays a normal biconcave disc; in the hypertonic solution (1.8%) water moves out and the cell shrinks and crenates. Solute particles are drawn as crowded as their concentration, with water particles in the room they leave.

title: U-tube osmosis: sucrose solution and water, before and after
description: A U-tube with a selectively permeable membrane at the bottom: side A holds 10% sucrose with gray sucrose particles and fewer blue water particles, side B holds pure water, the levels equal, with a water arrow from side B across the membrane to side A; then an arrow to the same U-tube with the level higher on side A and lower on side B
caption: A U-tube split at the bottom by a selectively permeable membrane, with 10% sucrose on side A and pure water on side B, the levels equal at the start. Sucrose can’t cross the membrane, so side A is hypertonic and water moves by osmosis from side B to side A. On the right the level has risen on side A and fallen on side B.

title: Red–green color blindness pedigree with X-linked genotypes
description: A three-generation pedigree titled Red–green color blindness, with an affected grandfather, carrier daughters drawn with a center dot, two affected grandsons, and each person’s genotype written on X and Y with B or b as a superscript
caption: A three-generation pedigree of 15 people. An affected grandfather, I-1, has two carrier daughters, II-2 and II-5, shown with a dot in the middle, and each has an affected son, III-1 and III-7; his son II-3 has unaffected children. Every person’s genotype is written on X and Y chromosomes with B and b as superscripts, and the key adds the carrier symbol.

title: Cystic fibrosis pedigree with blank genotypes (autosomal recessive)
description: A three-generation pedigree titled Cystic fibrosis, with two affected daughters, II-3 and III-4, both born to unaffected parents, and a blank line under each of the 13 people for a genotype
caption: A three-generation pedigree of 13 people. Unaffected parents I-1 and I-2 have an affected daughter, II-3, and a generation later unaffected II-5 and II-6 have an affected daughter, III-4; no one else is affected. Carriers aren’t marked, and a blank line under every person is for students to write the genotype, using F and f.

title: Hemophilia pedigree: X-linked recessive in a royal family
description: A four-generation pedigree titled Hemophilia in a royal family, with a half-filled carrier woman in generation I, seven affected men across generations II to IV, six more half-filled carrier women, deceased slashes, a proband arrow at IV-5 and a key
caption: A four-generation pedigree of 29 people, modeled on Queen Victoria’s family: a carrier woman, I-2, has an affected son, II-4, and two carrier daughters, II-3 and II-6. Every affected person is a man, seven in all across generations II to IV, and six of them are marked deceased. Carrier women are drawn half filled, the arrow marks the proband, IV-5, and the key below explains every symbol.

title: Huntington’s disease pedigree with genotypes (autosomal dominant)
description: A three-generation pedigree titled Huntington’s disease, with an affected deceased man in generation I, affected people in every generation, Hh or hh written under each person, a key, and the answer key line
caption: A three-generation pedigree of 17 people, starting with an affected man, I-1, marked deceased. Affected men and women appear in every generation, every affected child has an affected parent, and II-5 passes the trait to his son, III-6. Each person’s genotype is written under their number, Hh or hh, and the answer key line is printed under the key.

title: Y-linked pedigree: a random family over 3 generations
description: A three-generation pedigree of 18 people in which only I-1, his son II-2 and II-2’s sons III-1 and III-2 are affected, all men, with a key
caption: A random three-generation family of 18 people. The affected man in generation I, I-1, has an affected son, II-2, whose two sons, III-1 and III-2, are affected too; every woman is unaffected, and so are the sons of I-1’s daughters. There is no chart title, so the figure doesn’t give the trait away.

title: CO₂ and O₂ concentration around a plant in the light and then the dark
description: Graph against time in minutes, 0 to 60, on a grid, with CO₂ concentration (%) on the left axis and O₂ concentration (%) on the right: in the first 30 minutes, unshaded and labeled Light, the solid blue CO₂ line falls from 0.04 % toward 0.01 % while the dashed red O₂ line rises from 21 % to about 21.03 %; in the shaded half labeled Dark, CO₂ rises and O₂ falls in straight lines
caption: The CO₂ (solid blue, left axis) and O₂ (dashed red, right axis) in a closed chamber around a plant in bright light for 30 minutes, then in the dark, shaded. In the light, photosynthesis takes in CO₂ and gives off O₂ faster than respiration does the opposite, so the CO₂ falls and the O₂ rises by the same amount, both levelling off. In the dark the plant only respires: the CO₂ rises and the O₂ falls in straight lines.

title: CO₂ concentration in a closed chamber in the dark, dim and bright light
description: Graph of CO₂ concentration (%) against time (minutes) with no numbers on the axes: from one starting point, a solid blue line labeled Dark rises steadily, a dashed red line labeled Dim light (compensation point) stays level, and a dotted green line labeled Bright light falls and levels off near the bottom, with a key under the graph
caption: The CO₂ around a plant in a closed chamber over an hour, starting from the 0.04 % in air. In the dark (solid blue) the plant only respires, so the CO₂ rises in a straight line. In dim light at the compensation point (dashed red), photosynthesis uses just as much CO₂ as respiration gives off, so it stays level. In bright light (dotted green) it falls, then levels off at the CO₂ compensation point.

title: Limiting factors in photosynthesis: rate against light intensity at different CO₂ and temperatures
description: Graph of rate of photosynthesis against light intensity with no numbers on the axes: three curves rising together in a straight line, labeled Light is limiting, then levelling off at different heights, 0.1 % CO₂ at 25 °C (solid blue) highest, 0.1 % CO₂ at 15 °C (dashed red) lower and 0.04 % CO₂ at 15 °C (dotted green) lowest, with CO₂ or temperature is limiting written over the top plateau and a key under the graph
caption: The classic limiting-factor graph: the rate of photosynthesis against light intensity at 0.1 % CO₂ and 25 °C (solid blue), 0.1 % CO₂ and 15 °C (dashed red), and 0.04 % CO₂ and 15 °C (dotted green). At low light the three curves share one straight line, because light is limiting. Each then levels off where CO₂ or temperature limits the rate instead, highest with more CO₂ and the warmer temperature.

title: Limiting factors worksheet: what limits the rate of photosynthesis at A, B, C and D?
description: Black and white graph of rate of photosynthesis against light intensity with no numbers on the axes: a solid, a dashed and a dotted curve rising together and levelling off at three heights, with point A on the shared straight rise and points B, C and D on the three plateaus at the same light intensity, and a key naming 0.1 % CO₂ at 25 °C, 0.1 % CO₂ at 15 °C and 0.04 % CO₂ at 15 °C
caption: A black-and-white worksheet graph of the rate of photosynthesis against light intensity at three combinations of CO₂ and temperature. Point A is on the straight rise all three curves share; B, C and D are on their plateaus at the same light intensity, for questions like “What limits the rate at A?” and “Why is the rate at C lower than at B?”

title: Pondweed and lamp distance: bubbles of oxygen per minute against distance from the lamp
description: Graph of bubbles of oxygen per minute, 0 to 35, against distance from the lamp, 0 to 50 cm, on a grid: measured points scattered along a curve that stays level at about 27 bubbles a minute up to about 19 cm from the lamp, then falls, steeply at first and then more slowly, to about 4 bubbles a minute at 50 cm
caption: The pondweed practical: bubbles of oxygen counted each minute with the lamp 5 to 50 cm away, at 20 °C with plenty of CO₂. Close to the lamp the rate stays level, because light isn’t limiting. Farther away the light intensity falls as 1/d², so the rate falls with it, steeply at first and then more slowly. The points are scattered a little around the curve, like real counts.

title: Rate of photosynthesis against CO₂ concentration at high and low light intensity
description: Graph of rate of photosynthesis against CO₂ concentration (%) with no numbers on the axes: two curves rising together, the dashed red low light intensity curve levelling off early and low and the solid blue high light intensity curve rising further and levelling off about twice as high, with a key under the graph
caption: The rate of photosynthesis against CO₂ concentration at a high light intensity (solid blue) and a low one (dashed red), both at 25 °C. At first more CO₂ speeds photosynthesis up whatever the light, so the curves rise together. Then each levels off where light becomes the limiting factor, the dimly lit plant at a much lower rate and lower CO₂ concentration.

title: Rate of photosynthesis against temperature at high and low light intensity
description: Graph of rate of photosynthesis against temperature (°C) with no numbers on the axes: a solid blue high light intensity curve rising to a peak marked Optimum with a dot and a dashed line down to the axis, then falling steeply to zero, and a dashed red low light intensity curve with a low flat top that follows it down at both ends
caption: The rate of photosynthesis against temperature in high light (solid blue) and low light (dashed red), at 0.1 % CO₂. In bright light the rate follows the enzymes: it rises to an optimum near 30 °C, marked, then falls steeply as they denature. In dim light the curve has a low, flat top, because light limits the rate whatever the temperature; only where it is cold or the enzymes denature does it fall away.

title: Blank population growth graph for students to draw on
description: Blank graph of population size (N) from 0 to 1100 against time in years from 0 to 20, with only a dashed line at 1000 labeled Carrying capacity (K)
caption: Empty axes for students to sketch a population’s growth: population size (N) up to 1100 against time from 0 to 20 years. Only the carrying capacity is drawn, a dashed line at 1000 labeled Carrying capacity (K), so students can draw the S-curve leveling off at it, or an exponential J-curve to compare.

title: Exponential vs. logistic growth graph (J-curve and S-curve)
description: Graph of population size over 20 years with a dashed red J-shaped curve labeled Exponential growth running off the top and a blue S-shaped curve labeled Logistic growth leveling off at a dashed carrying capacity line at 1000
caption: Exponential and logistic growth from the same starting population of 10 and the same r, 0.5 per year, graphed over 20 years. The two curves match at first; then the dashed exponential J-curve shoots off the top of the graph, while the logistic S-curve slows and levels off at the carrying capacity, 1000.

title: Growth rate and per capita growth rate vs. population size
description: Two stacked graphs against population size N from 0 to 1100: the growth rate dN/dt as a hump peaking at 125 individuals per year at N = 500, labeled Fastest growth (N = K/2), and the per capita growth rate falling in a straight line from 0.5 to 0, with a dashed carrying capacity line at 1000 on both
caption: Logistic growth with r = 0.5 per year and K = 1000, graphed against population size. On top, the growth rate dN/dt is a hump that is 0 at N = 0 and at K, with its peak marked at N = K/2. Below, the per capita growth rate falls in a straight line from 0.5 to 0 at the carrying capacity, which is a dashed line on both graphs.

title: Logistic growth curve with carrying capacity (S-curve)
description: S-shaped logistic growth curve of a deer population rising from 20 and leveling off at a dashed carrying capacity line at 500, labeled Carrying capacity (K), with the inflection point at 250 deer marked by a dot
caption: The logistic growth of a deer population on an island over 30 years, starting from 20 deer with r = 0.4 per year and a carrying capacity of 500. The S-shaped curve speeds up, then slows and levels off along the dashed carrying capacity line. The inflection point is marked with a dot and dashed lines to the axes where the population reaches 250, half of K.

title: Yeast population growth curve with census data and growth phases
description: Logistic growth curve of yeast cells in thousands over 18 hours with hourly census dots scattered near it, a dashed carrying capacity line at 665, and brackets above labeled Lag phase, Exponential phase and Stationary phase
caption: Yeast growing in a flask over 18 hours, from 10 thousand cells at 0.54 per hour toward a carrying capacity of 665 thousand. Census counts taken every hour are scattered by about 5% around the logistic curve, like real lab data. Brackets above the graph mark the lag, exponential and stationary phases, with dotted lines down the graph where each ends.

title: Hare and lynx census data graph
description: Graph of yearly census counts of hares (blue dots joined by a solid line) and lynx (red open squares joined by a dashed line), in thousands, over 40 years, rising and falling in four uneven cycles
caption: Census counts of snowshoe hares (blue dots) and Canada lynx (red squares), in thousands, taken once a year for 40 years and joined by lines, solid for hares and dashed for lynx. Each count is off by about 10%, the way a real census is, so the peaks come out uneven, but the lynx still peak after the hares in every cycle.

title: Snowshoe hare and lynx population graph with lag and period
description: Graph of snowshoe hare and Canada lynx populations in thousands over 40 years, hares a solid blue line and lynx a dashed red line, each peak marked with a dot and a dotted line, with arrows labeled “Lag: 1.6 years” and “Period: 10 years”
caption: Snowshoe hares (solid blue) and Canada lynx (dashed red), in thousands, over 40 years, from the Lotka–Volterra model. Both populations rise and fall in a repeating cycle, the lynx peaking a little after the hares. Each peak has a dot with a dotted line down to the time axis, and arrows mark the lag from a hare peak to the next lynx peak (1.6 years) and the period from one hare peak to the next (10 years).

title: Moose and wolf population cycles graph (Isle Royale)
description: Graph of moose (solid blue line, left axis 0 to 1800) and wolves (dashed red line, right axis 0 to 45) over 90 years, three cycles, each peak marked with a dot and a dotted line down to the time axis
caption: Moose (solid blue) and wolves (dashed red) over 90 years, moose on the left axis and wolves on the right, from the model with classroom numbers for the moose and wolves of Isle Royale rather than real counts. The cycle is long and slow, the wolves peaking several years after the moose, and every peak is marked with a dot and a dotted line down to the time axis so students can read when it happens.

title: Predator–prey graph worksheet: find the lag and period
description: Black and white graph of rabbits (solid line, left axis 0 to 1000) and foxes (dashed line, right axis 0 to 100) over 20 years, with arrows labeled “Lag:” and “Period:” followed by blank lines
caption: Rabbits (solid line) and red foxes (dashed line) over 20 years, in black and white, with rabbits counted on the left axis and foxes on the right. One arrow spans from a rabbit peak to the fox peak after it and another from one rabbit peak to the next, labeled “Lag:” and “Period:” with blank lines for students to fill in from the time axis.

title: Predator–prey phase plane: lynx against hares
description: Phase plane graph with hares (thousands) on the x-axis and lynx (thousands) on the y-axis: a closed blue loop with four arrows going round it counterclockwise
caption: The same hare and lynx cycle drawn as a phase plane: lynx against hares, both in thousands, over one full cycle. The populations trace a closed loop that goes round counterclockwise, the way the arrows point: hares rise while lynx are few, lynx rise as hares peak, hares fall while lynx are many, and lynx fall while hares are few. One trip round the loop is one cycle.

title: Blank ABO blood type Punnett square worksheet (codominance)
description: A blank Punnett square under a question about blood type, with Mother Iᴬi across the top and Father Iᴮi down the side, gametes Iᴬ and i and Iᴮ and i, four empty cells, and blank lines for the genotype and phenotype ratios
caption: A Punnett square worksheet on ABO blood type, with a question above it: a mother with type A blood and a father with type B blood each carry the allele for type O. The parents are labeled Mother Iᴬi and Father Iᴮi, with gametes Iᴬ and i across the top and Iᴮ and i down the side, and the four cells are left empty for students. Blank lines follow for the genotype and phenotype ratios.

title: Color blindness Punnett square: X-linked cross of a carrier mother
description: An X-linked Punnett square crossing ♀ XᴮXᵇ × ♂ XᴮY, with gametes Xᴮ and Xᵇ across the top and Xᴮ and Y down the side, offspring XᴮXᴮ, XᴮXᵇ, XᴮY and XᵇY, the color-blind cell shaded gray, and percentages for genotypes, daughters and sons below
caption: An X-linked Punnett square for red-green color blindness: a carrier mother, ♀ XᴮXᵇ, across the top and a father with normal vision, ♂ XᴮY, down the side. The cells hold two daughters, XᴮXᴮ and XᴮXᵇ, and two sons, XᴮY and XᵇY, with the color-blind cell shaded gray and a key. Under the square the genotypes are given as percentages, then the phenotypes separately for daughters and for sons.

title: Dihybrid cross Punnett square: RrYy × RrYy
description: A 4 by 4 Punnett square crossing RrYy × RrYy with gametes RY, Ry, rY and ry on each side, 16 offspring genotypes shaded by phenotype, a key for round yellow, round green, wrinkled yellow and wrinkled green, and the genotype and phenotype ratios below
caption: A 4 × 4 dihybrid Punnett square crossing two pea plants heterozygous for seed shape and seed color, RrYy × RrYy. Each parent’s four gametes, RY, Ry, rY and ry, run across the top and down the side, and the 16 cells hold the offspring genotypes. Each phenotype has its own fill, with a key: gray for round yellow, hatching for round green, dots for wrinkled yellow, and white for wrinkled green. Both ratios are printed below.

title: Incomplete dominance Punnett square: snapdragon flower color
description: A Punnett square crossing two pink snapdragons, CᴿCᵂ × CᴿCᵂ, with offspring CᴿCᴿ red, CᴿCᵂ pink, CᴿCᵂ pink and CᵂCᵂ white, red shaded gray, pink hatched, white unshaded, a key, and the genotype and phenotype ratios below
caption: A Punnett square for snapdragon flower color, a classic case of incomplete dominance: two pink parents, CᴿCᵂ × CᴿCᵂ, with gametes Cᴿ and Cᵂ on each side. Each cell gives its genotype with the flower color written under it, and each color has its own fill: gray for red, hatching for pink and white left unshaded, with a key. The genotype and phenotype ratios are printed below.

title: Tt × Tt Punnett square: monohybrid cross for pea plant height
description: A Punnett square titled Pea plant height crossing Tt × Tt, with gametes T and t on each side, offspring TT, Tt, Tt and tt, the tall cells shaded gray, a key for tall and short, and the genotype and phenotype ratios below
caption: A Punnett square for Mendel’s pea plants under the chart title “Pea plant height”: Tt across the top and Tt down the side, with gametes T and t on each edge and the offspring TT, Tt, Tt and tt in the four cells. The tall cells are shaded gray and the short one left white, with a key below. The genotype and phenotype ratios are printed under the square.

title: Blank Bohr model to fill in (aluminum)
description: Bohr model of aluminum with 13 protons and 14 neutrons in the nucleus and three empty rings labeled n = 1 to n = 3
caption: A Bohr model worksheet figure for aluminum: the nucleus shows 13 protons and 14 neutrons, and three empty rings labeled n = 1, n = 2 and n = 3. Students draw the electrons themselves: 2, 8 and 3.

title: Bohr model of calcium (Ca)
description: Bohr model of a calcium atom: a nucleus labeled 20 protons and 20 neutrons, with 2, 8, 8 and 2 electrons on four shells
caption: A Bohr model of a neutral calcium atom, with its nucleus written as text: 20 protons and 20 neutrons. Its 20 electrons fill four shells as 2, 8, 8 and 2. The two electrons on the outer shell are calcium’s valence electrons.

title: Bohr model of carbon (C)
description: Bohr model of a carbon atom: 6 protons and 6 neutrons in the nucleus, 2 and 4 electrons on two shells, with a key
caption: A Bohr model of a neutral carbon-12 atom: 6 protons and 6 neutrons in the nucleus, and 6 electrons, 2 on the first shell and 4 on the second. A key beside it shows which dot is a proton, a neutron and an electron.

title: Bohr model of a chloride ion (Cl⁻)
description: Bohr model of a chloride ion in brackets with a − charge: 17 protons, 18 neutrons, and 2, 8 and 8 electrons with the gained electron in green
caption: A Bohr model of the chloride ion Cl⁻, in square brackets with its 1− charge. It has 17 protons, 18 neutrons and 18 electrons on three shells as 2, 8 and 8. The one electron gained to complete the outer shell is drawn in green, and a key explains the colors.

title: Bohr model of oxygen (O)
description: Bohr model of an oxygen atom: 8 protons and 8 neutrons, with 2 electrons on the first shell and 6 on the second drawn in pairs
caption: A Bohr model of a neutral oxygen atom with 8 protons and 8 neutrons in the nucleus. Its 8 electrons are 2 on the first shell and 6 on the second, drawn in pairs at the four compass points as in a Lewis structure, so the two unpaired valence electrons stand out. The shells are labeled n = 1 and n = 2.

title: Bohr model of sodium (Na)
description: Bohr model of a sodium atom: a nucleus of 11 protons and 12 neutrons, with 2, 8 and 1 electrons on three shells
caption: A Bohr model of a neutral sodium atom. The nucleus is drawn as 11 red protons and 12 gray neutrons, and 11 blue electrons sit on three rings: 2 on the first shell, 8 on the second and 1 on the third. The single outer electron is sodium’s one valence electron.

title: Bohr model of a sodium ion (Na⁺)
description: Bohr model of a sodium ion in brackets with a + charge: 11 protons, 12 neutrons and 2 and 8 electrons, the lost third-shell electron drawn as an empty dashed spot
caption: A Bohr model of the sodium ion Na⁺, in square brackets with its 1+ charge at the top right. It has 11 protons and 12 neutrons but only 10 electrons, 2 and 8. The electron it lost from the third shell is drawn as an empty dashed spot on the third ring, and a key explains the symbols.

title: Find the mistake: dot-and-cross diagram of sodium chloride (NaCl)
description: A deliberately wrong dot-and-cross diagram of sodium chloride: a sodium ion with 8 crosses and a chloride ion with only 7 dots, its gained electron missing, each in square brackets with its charge
caption: A deliberately wrong dot-and-cross diagram of sodium chloride, NaCl, for a “find the mistake” question. The chloride ion is drawn with only its own 7 electrons as dots, so the electron it gained from sodium is missing: Cl⁻ should have 8 electrons on its outer shell, 7 dots and 1 cross, to match its 1− charge.

title: Dot-and-cross diagram of a calcium atom (2, 8, 8, 2)
description: A calcium atom drawn as four shells around the symbol Ca, with 2, 8, 8 and 2 electrons as dots
caption: A calcium atom, Ca, with every shell drawn as a circle around its symbol and its 20 electrons as dots: 2, 8, 8 and 2 from the inside out. The electrons are paired at the top, right, bottom and left of each ring, as students are taught to draw an electron arrangement.

title: Dot-and-cross diagram of aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃)
description: Dot-and-cross diagram of aluminum oxide: 2 in front of a bracketed Al³⁺ ion with 8 crosses, and 3 in front of a bracketed O²⁻ ion with 6 dots and 2 crosses
caption: A dot-and-cross diagram of aluminum oxide, Al₂O₃, drawn as one of each ion with its number in front: 2[Al]³⁺ and 3[O]²⁻. Each aluminum ion has 8 crosses on its outer shell, and each oxide ion its own 6 electrons as dots and the 2 it gained as crosses.

title: Dot-and-cross diagram of carbon dioxide (CO₂)
description: Dot-and-cross diagram of carbon dioxide: a carbon circle between two oxygen circles, each overlap holding two dots and two crosses, and two lone pairs of crosses on each oxygen
caption: A dot-and-cross diagram of carbon dioxide, CO₂, with a double bond to each oxygen: each overlap holds two shared pairs, two dots from the carbon and two crosses from the oxygen. Each oxygen also has two lone pairs of crosses on its own circle.

title: Dot-and-cross diagram of ethanol (C₂H₅OH)
description: Dot-and-cross diagram of ethanol: two carbon circles and an oxygen circle in a row, overlapped by six smaller hydrogen circles, each overlap holding one shared pair, with two lone pairs on the oxygen
caption: A dot-and-cross diagram of ethanol, C₂H₅OH. Each carbon’s electrons and the oxygen’s have their own mark, dots, open circles and open squares, and the hydrogens’ are crosses, so every shared pair shows which atom gave each electron. The hydrogen circles are drawn a little smaller so the hydrogens on the two carbons don’t overlap each other.

title: Dot-and-cross diagram of ethene (C₂H₄) for students to complete
description: The overlapping outer shells of ethene, two carbons and four hydrogens, with no electrons drawn, and an answer key under them
caption: The outer shells of ethene, C₂H₄, drawn with no electrons, for students to add them: two overlapping carbon circles, each overlapped by two hydrogen circles. The answer key under it gives each atom’s bonding pairs, four for each carbon, including the double bond, and one for each hydrogen.

title: Dot-and-cross diagram of magnesium chloride (MgCl₂)
description: Dot-and-cross diagram of magnesium chloride: a magnesium ion with 8 crosses between two chloride ions, each with 7 dots and 1 cross, in brackets with their charges, and an answer key
caption: A dot-and-cross diagram of magnesium chloride, MgCl₂, with every ion drawn: Cl⁻ Mg²⁺ Cl⁻, the magnesium ion in the middle. Each chloride ion has the cross it gained from magnesium on the side facing it. The answer key under it says how the electrons moved and gives each ion’s electron arrangement.

title: Dot-and-cross diagram of methane (CH₄)
description: Dot-and-cross diagram of methane: a carbon circle overlapped by four hydrogen circles above, below, left and right, each overlap holding a dot and a cross
caption: A dot-and-cross diagram of methane, CH₄. The carbon atom’s outer shell overlaps the shells of four hydrogen atoms on its four sides, and each overlap holds one shared pair, a dot from the carbon and a cross from the hydrogen. The carbon has no lone pairs and ends with 8 electrons.

title: Dot-and-cross diagram of nitrogen (N₂)
description: Dot-and-cross diagram of a nitrogen molecule: two overlapping circles with three dots and three crosses in the overlap and one lone pair on each atom
caption: A dot-and-cross diagram of a nitrogen molecule, N₂, with its triple bond: three shared pairs in the overlap, each a dot from one nitrogen and a cross from the other. Each nitrogen has one lone pair on the far side of its circle.

title: Dot-and-cross diagram of sodium chloride (NaCl)
description: Dot-and-cross diagram of sodium chloride: a sodium ion with 8 crosses and a chloride ion with 7 dots and 1 cross, each in square brackets with its charge
caption: A dot-and-cross diagram of sodium chloride, NaCl. The sodium ion, Na⁺, is drawn with the full shell it is left with, 8 crosses, and the chloride ion, Cl⁻, with its own 7 electrons as dots and the one it gained from sodium as a cross. Each ion is in square brackets with its charge at the top right.

title: Dot-and-cross diagram of water (H₂O)
description: Dot-and-cross diagram of water: an oxygen circle overlapping two hydrogen circles, a dot and a cross in each overlap, and two lone pairs of dots on the oxygen
caption: A dot-and-cross diagram of a water molecule, H₂O, outer shells only. The oxygen atom’s circle overlaps each hydrogen atom’s, and each overlap holds one shared pair: a dot from the oxygen and a cross from the hydrogen. The oxygen’s two lone pairs of dots sit on its own circle, so it has 8 electrons and each hydrogen 2.

title: 50 cm³ gas syringe reading 23.5 cm³
description: A 50 cm³ gas syringe on its own, its plunger at 23.5 cm³, with a magnified view
caption: A 50 cm³ gas syringe on its own, marked every 1 cm³ and numbered every 10 cm³ from 0 at the nozzle. The plunger’s face is halfway between 23 and 24 cm³, so the reading is 23.5 cm³. A magnified view above shows the face against the marks.

title: Gas syringe collecting gas: 64.0 cm³
description: A conical flask joined by a delivery tube to a 100 cm³ gas syringe on a stand, reading 64.0 cm³, with a magnified view of the plunger
caption: A conical flask of liquid, closed with a bung and joined by a delivery tube to a 100 cm³ gas syringe clamped on a stand. The gas has pushed the plunger out to the 64 cm³ mark, so 64.0 cm³ of gas has been collected. A magnified view above the syringe shows the plunger’s face against the marks.

title: Gas syringe plunger close-up: 37.6 cm³
description: A magnified view of a gas syringe’s scale, the plunger’s face at 37.6 cm³
caption: Only the magnified view of a 100 cm³ gas syringe, showing the plunger’s flat face between the 37 and 38 cm³ marks. It is a little past halfway, so the reading is 37.6 cm³. Use it to practice reading at the plunger’s face rather than its knob.

title: Gas syringe reading in mL: 31.8 mL
description: A conical flask joined by a delivery tube to a 50 mL gas syringe on a stand, its scale in mL, the plunger at 31.8 mL
caption: A conical flask joined by a delivery tube to a 50 mL gas syringe clamped on a stand, its scale printed in mL and drawn without a magnifier. The plunger’s face is most of the way from the 31 to the 32 mL mark, read as 31.8 mL of gas. mL and cm³ are the same size, so this is also 31.8 cm³.

title: Carbon-14 decaying to nitrogen-14: parent and daughter
description: Carbon-14 falling and nitrogen-14 rising as percent of atoms against time in years, crossing at 50% at one half-life, marked T½
caption: Carbon-14, the parent, falls from 100% of the atoms while its stable daughter, nitrogen-14, rises from 0%, the daughter dashed and both named in a key. The two always add up to 100%, so they cross at 50% after one half-life, where a dashed guide line labeled T½ runs down to the time axis.

title: Carbon-14 half-life graph
description: Decay curve of carbon-14, percent remaining against time in years, with dashed guide lines at 5,730, 11,460 and 17,190 years
caption: The percent of carbon-14 remaining against time in years, from 100% at the start, on an axis numbered every 4,000 years up to 30,000. Dashed guide lines run from 50%, 25% and 12.5% across to the curve and down to the time axis, each labeled with its time: 5,730, 11,460 and 17,190 years, one, two and three half-lives.

title: Identify the isotope from its half-life: three decay curves
description: Three decay curves, solid, dashed and dotted, named Isotope A, Isotope B and Isotope C in a key, against time in years from 0 to 160
caption: Three radioactive isotopes decaying on one graph, percent remaining against time in years. The curves are solid, dashed and dotted so they read apart in black and white, and the key calls them only Isotope A, B and C. Students read each half-life off the curve where it crosses 50% and match the isotopes to a table of half-lives.

title: Iodine-131 decay: mass remaining over 45 days
description: Decay curve of an 80 g sample of iodine-131, mass remaining in grams against time in days, with a dot at the start and at each half-life
caption: An 80 g sample of iodine-131 decaying over 45 days, its mass remaining in grams against time in days. A dot marks the start and each half-life along the curve, at 80, 40, 20, 10, 5 and 2.5 g, for questions on how much is left after a given time.

title: Plot the decay curve: Isotope X, half-life 10 years
description: Dots at 100, 50, 25, 12.5, 6.25 and 3.125 percent every 10 years on an empty grid, for students to join into a decay curve
caption: The points of a made-up Isotope X with a half-life of 10 years, its percent remaining at the start and after each half-life, 100%, 50%, 25%, 12.5% and so on, with the curve left off. Students join the dots with a smooth curve and see that it never reaches zero.

title: Technetium-99m activity: read the half-life
description: Activity of technetium-99m in becquerels from 800 Bq against time in hours, with dashed guide lines from 400 and 200 Bq and blank lines by the time axis
caption: The activity of a technetium-99m sample, the medical tracer, falling from 800 Bq, against time in hours. Dashed guide lines run from 400 Bq and 200 Bq across to the curve and down to the time axis, each with a blank line for students to write the time, one and two half-lives.

title: Cooling curve of water
description: Cooling curve of water from steam at 120 °C to ice at −20 °C, with plateaus labeled Condensing at 100 °C and Freezing at 0 °C
caption: The temperature of water cooled steadily from steam at 120 °C to ice at −20 °C, against time. The curve falls through the gas, stays flat at 100 °C while the steam condenses, falls through the liquid, stays flat at 0 °C while the water freezes, then falls through the solid. The sloped segments are labeled with their states and the plateaus with the changes, and the temperatures are written by the dashed lines.

title: Cooling curve with supercooling
description: Cooling curve of water from 80 °C to −20 °C that dips 5 °C below the freezing point before rising back to 0 °C and freezing, corners lettered A to D
caption: The temperature of water cooled steadily from 80 °C to −20 °C, against time. The liquid cools past its freezing point to −5 °C before ice starts to form, then the heat given out as it freezes warms it back up to 0 °C, written by the dashed line, where it stays until it has frozen. Its corners are lettered A to D.

title: Heating curve of ethanol
description: Heating curve of ethanol from −140 °C to 100 °C, with plateaus at its melting point, −114.1 °C, and boiling point, 78.3 °C, written by the temperature axis
caption: The temperature of ethanol heated steadily from −140 °C to 100 °C, against time. It melts at −114.1 °C and boils at 78.3 °C, each written by the temperature axis above the dashed line from its plateau. The sloped segments are labeled with their states and the plateaus with the changes.

title: Heating curve of water, lettered A to F
description: Heating curve of water from ice at −20 °C to steam at 120 °C, with plateaus at 0 and 100 °C labeled Melting and Boiling, corners lettered A to F
caption: The temperature of water heated steadily from ice at −20 °C to steam at 120 °C, against time. The curve rises through the solid, stays flat at 0 °C while the ice melts, rises through the liquid, stays flat at 100 °C while the water boils, then rises through the gas. Its corners are lettered A to F, the sloped segments are labeled with their states and the plateaus with the changes, and dashed lines run from the plateaus to the temperature axis, with 0 °C and 100 °C written by them.

title: Heating curve of water to scale, against heat added
description: Heating curve of 100 g of water against heat added in kJ, its boiling plateau much longer than its melting plateau, with blank lines to label each segment
caption: The temperature of 100 g of water heated from ice at −20 °C to steam at 120 °C, against the heat added in kJ, drawn to scale from water’s specific heats and enthalpies of fusion and vaporization. The boiling plateau at 100 °C is almost seven times as long as the melting plateau at 0 °C, each temperature written by its dashed line. Each segment has a blank line for students to name its state.

title: Heating curve worksheet: label the melting and boiling points
description: Heating curve of an unknown substance from 0 °C to 160 °C, its corners lettered A to F, with blank lines for the segment labels and by the temperature axis at each plateau
caption: The temperature of an unknown substance, Substance X, heated steadily from 0 °C to 160 °C, against time, with plateaus at 40 °C and 120 °C. Its corners are lettered A to F, and every segment and both plateaus’ dashed lines have blank lines, for students to name each state and change and to mark the melting and boiling points.

title: Caliper reading 23.45 mm
description: A caliper holding a block, reading 23.45 mm on its 0.05 mm sliding scale, with a close-up strip of its scales
caption: A 150 mm caliper with a block held between its outside jaws. The close-up strip below it shows the sliding scale’s zero just past 23 mm on the main scale, and its 9th mark, between the 4 and the 5, lined up with a main-scale mark: 23 + 9 × 0.05 = 23.45 mm. The least count, 0.05 mm, is printed on the slider.

title: Caliper with a zero error
description: Two 0.1 mm calipers: above, with its jaws closed, reading 0.3 mm; below, holding block A, reading 27.6 mm, each with a close-up strip of its scales
caption: The same 0.1 mm caliper twice. Above, with its jaws closed, the sliding scale’s zero sits just past the main scale’s zero and its 3rd mark lines up: a zero error of +0.3 mm. Below, holding block A, it reads 27.6 mm. Students take the zero error off the reading: the block is 27.3 mm long.

title: Ruler marked only in centimeters: 5.3 cm
description: A 15 cm ruler marked only every centimeter, with a cube lying along it from 0 to 5.3 cm
caption: A 15 cm ruler with marks only every whole centimeter and a cube lying along it from 0. Its right end is about three tenths of the way from 5 to 6 cm, so its length is 5.3 cm, with the tenths digit estimated. Compare it with a millimeter ruler to show how the marks set the significant figures.

title: Inch ruler reading 3 5/16 inches
description: A 6 inch ruler marked in sixteenths with a row of marbles from 0 to 3 5/16 inches
caption: A 6 inch ruler marked every sixteenth of an inch, with marks shortening from halves down to sixteenths. A row of three marbles lies along it from 0, with dashed guide lines down from its ends. Its right end is on the 3 5/16 inch mark, so the row is 3 5/16 inches long.

title: Meter stick reading 62.4 cm
description: A meter stick marked every centimeter with a long metal cylinder lying along it from 0 to 62.4 cm
caption: A meter stick (100 cm) marked every centimeter and numbered every 5 cm, with a long metal cylinder lying along it from 0. Its right end falls between 62 and 63 cm, read as 62.4 cm with the tenths digit estimated. A magnified view shows the right end against the marks.

title: Metric ruler reading 7.45 cm
description: A 15 cm ruler marked in millimeters with a metal cylinder lying along it from 0 to 7.45 cm, with a magnified view of its right end
caption: A 15 cm ruler marked every millimeter, with a metal cylinder lying along it, its left end on 0. Its right end falls halfway between 7.4 and 7.5 cm, so its length is 7.45 cm, the hundredths digit estimated. A magnified view shows the right end against the marks.

title: Micrometer reading estimated to 0.001 mm: 6.847 mm
description: A micrometer holding a cylinder, reading 6.847 mm, with a magnified view showing the datum line between the thimble’s 34th and 35th marks
caption: A micrometer read one digit past its marks. The magnifier shows the 6.5 mm mark uncovered below the sleeve’s datum line, and the datum line about 0.7 of the way from the thimble’s 34th mark to its 35th, so the reading is 6.5 + 0.347 = 6.847 mm. The last digit is estimated, so 6.846 or 6.848 mm is as good an answer.

title: Micrometer reading just past half a millimeter: 5.51 mm
description: A micrometer holding a wire, reading 5.51 mm, with a magnified view showing the 5.5 mm mark just uncovered on the sleeve
caption: A micrometer measuring a wire, with the thimble’s edge just past the 5.5 mm mark below the sleeve’s datum line, and the thimble’s 1st mark on the datum line. The reading is 5.5 + 0.01 = 5.51 mm. Missing the half-millimeter mark would give 5.01 mm, the common mistake.

title: Micrometer with a negative zero error
description: Two micrometers: above, closed, its thimble’s 0 three marks above the datum line, reading −0.03 mm; below, holding a wire, reading 3.27 mm, each with a magnified view
caption: The same micrometer twice. Above, closed, the thimble’s 0 has turned three marks past the datum line, so it reads −0.03 mm: a negative zero error. Below, holding a wire, it reads 3.27 mm. Taking off the zero error gives 3.27 − (−0.03) = 3.30 mm.

title: Measuring with a ruler not starting at zero
description: A 15 cm ruler with a rock lying along it from 2.00 cm to 8.35 cm, with magnified views of both ends
caption: A 15 cm millimeter ruler with a rock lying along it, starting at the 2 cm mark rather than 0, with dashed lines dropped from its ends to the ruler. Magnified views show its left end at 2.00 cm and its right end at 8.35 cm. Its length is the difference, 6.35 cm.

title: Lewis dot diagram of the nitride ion (N³⁻)
description: Lewis dot diagram of the nitride ion: N with a pair of dots on each of its four sides, in square brackets with a 3− charge
caption: The Lewis dot diagram of the nitride ion, N³⁻. A nitrogen atom has 5 valence electrons and gains 3 to fill its octet, so the symbol has a pair of dots on each of its four sides, 8 electrons in all. It is drawn in square brackets with its 3− charge.

title: Lewis dot structure of CH₄ (methane)
description: Lewis dot structure of methane: a carbon with a pair of dots to each of four hydrogens
caption: The Lewis dot structure of methane, CH₄, with each bond drawn as a pair of dots rather than a line. The carbon shares one pair of electrons with each of four hydrogen atoms, 8 valence electrons in all, and has no lone pairs.

title: Lewis structure of CO₂ (carbon dioxide)
description: Lewis structure of CO2: O=C=O with two double bonds and two lone pairs on each oxygen
caption: The Lewis structure of carbon dioxide, CO₂: a carbon atom in the middle joined to each oxygen by a double bond. Each oxygen has two lone pairs and the carbon none, for 16 valence electrons in all, and every atom has an octet.

title: Lewis structure of H₂O (water)
description: Lewis structure of water drawn bent: an oxygen with two lone pairs single-bonded to two hydrogens
caption: The Lewis structure of water, H₂O: an oxygen atom single-bonded to two hydrogen atoms, with two lone pairs on the oxygen. It is drawn bent, hinting at the molecule’s real shape, and shows all 8 valence electrons.

title: Lewis structure of HCN (hydrogen cyanide)
description: Lewis structure of HCN: H single-bonded to C, triple-bonded to N with one lone pair
caption: The Lewis structure of hydrogen cyanide, HCN: hydrogen single-bonded to a central carbon, which is triple-bonded to nitrogen. The nitrogen has one lone pair, for 10 valence electrons in all.

title: Lewis structure of NH₃ (ammonia)
description: Lewis structure of ammonia: a nitrogen with one lone pair single-bonded to three hydrogens spread below it
caption: The Lewis structure of ammonia, NH₃: a nitrogen atom single-bonded to three hydrogen atoms, with one lone pair on top. The hydrogens are spread below the nitrogen to hint at its trigonal pyramidal shape. It shows all 8 valence electrons.

title: Lewis structure of sulfate (SO₄²⁻)
description: Lewis structure of the sulfate ion: sulfur single-bonded to four oxygens, each with three lone pairs, in brackets with a 2− charge and formal charges
caption: The Lewis structure of the sulfate ion, SO₄²⁻, following the octet rule: sulfur single-bonded to four oxygen atoms, each oxygen with three lone pairs. The structure is in square brackets with the 2− charge, and formal charges are shown (+2 on sulfur, −1 on each oxygen).

title: Resonance structures of nitrate (NO₃⁻)
description: The three resonance structures of the nitrate ion in brackets, joined by double-headed arrows, with formal charges
caption: The three resonance structures of the nitrate ion, NO₃⁻, side by side and joined by double-headed arrows. In each, nitrogen has one double bond and two single bonds to oxygen, and only the position of the double bond changes. Each is in square brackets with the ion’s 1− charge, and formal charges are shown.

title: Absorption spectra of hydrogen and helium
description: Absorption spectra of hydrogen and helium: dark lines across a continuous rainbow from 400 to 700 nm
caption: The absorption spectra of hydrogen and helium, each a continuous rainbow from violet at 400 nm to red at 700 nm crossed by black lines where the gas absorbs light. The dark lines sit at exactly the wavelengths of each element’s bright emission lines, the way elements are identified in the light of stars.

title: Emission spectra of hydrogen, helium and sodium with an unknown to identify
description: Bright-line emission spectra of hydrogen, helium and sodium stacked on one 400–700 nm wavelength scale, with an unknown spectrum under them made of two of the three
caption: Three bright-line emission spectra, hydrogen, helium and sodium, drawn as colored lines on black and stacked on one wavelength scale from 400 to 700 nm, so a line at the same wavelength sits at the same place in every strip. The fourth strip, labeled Unknown, is a mixture: it shows every line of hydrogen and of sodium, for students to match against the three above.

title: Emission spectra of flame test metals: lithium, sodium, strontium and copper
description: Bright-line emission spectra of lithium, sodium, strontium and copper on one wavelength scale, with an unknown made of two of them
caption: Bright-line emission spectra of four metals used in flame tests, lithium, sodium, strontium and copper, each with a few of its strongest visible lines, on one 400 to 700 nm scale. Under them, an unknown shows every line of sodium and of strontium for students to identify.

title: Hydrogen emission spectrum: the Balmer series
description: The bright-line emission spectrum of hydrogen from 400 to 700 nm: four lines, violet, blue-violet, cyan and red
caption: The visible emission spectrum of hydrogen, the Balmer series, as four colored lines on black on a 400 to 700 nm scale: a violet line, a blue-violet line, a cyan line and a red line. Each is light given off as hydrogen’s electron falls to the second energy level, the lines students connect to the Bohr model.

title: Identify the element: black-and-white line spectra with blank labels
description: Three line spectra drawn as black lines on white, each with a blank line in place of the element’s name
caption: Three line spectra, mercury, neon and helium, printed as black lines on white for a black-and-white copier, each with a blank line where the element’s name would be. Students match the line positions on the 400 to 700 nm scale to a reference chart to name each element.

title: Line spectra of made-up elements X, Y and Z with an unknown
description: Emission spectra of three made-up elements, X, Y and Z, each with three lines, and an unknown made of two of them
caption: Emission spectra of three made-up elements, X, Y and Z, each drawn with three lines typed in by the teacher, so students can’t look the answer up. The Unknown strip under them shows every line of Element X and Element Z, and students identify it by matching lines.

title: Analytical balance reading 0.2537 g
description: An analytical balance inside its glass draft shield, its display reading 0.2537 g
caption: An analytical balance inside its glass draft shield, with a weigh boat on the pan and the display reading 0.2537 g. It shows four decimal places, a tenth of a milligram, so its reading has four significant figures here.

title: Mass of a metal cube on a digital balance
description: A metal cube on a digital balance showing 21.6 g
caption: A metal cube sits on the pan of a digital balance that shows one decimal place, reading 21.6 g. With the cube’s volume from a displacement or ruler figure, students can find its density.

title: Digital balance reading 12.47 g
description: A digital balance with a weigh boat on its pan, its display reading 12.47 g
caption: A digital balance with a weigh boat on its pan, its display showing 12.47 g. A digital balance is read exactly as shown, to its two decimal places, with no estimated digit.

title: Triple beam balance reading 263.47 g
description: A triple beam balance with its riders at 200 g, 60 g and 3.47 g, with a magnified view of the front beam
caption: A triple beam balance with its three riders at 200 g on the beam marked in hundreds, 60 g on the beam marked in tens, and 3.47 g on the bottom beam, marked every 0.1 g from 0 to 10. The mass is their sum, 263.47 g, with the hundredths digit estimated. A magnified view shows the bottom rider against its marks.

title: Mass of a rock on a triple beam balance
description: A rock on the pan of a triple beam balance with its riders reading 72.35 g
caption: A rock sits on the pan of a triple beam balance with its riders at 70 g on the tens beam, 0 g on the hundreds beam and 2.35 g on the bottom beam. The rock’s mass is their sum, 72.35 g. Pair it with a volume by displacement figure for a density question.

title: Draw the missing peak: silicon mass spectrum
description: The mass spectrum of silicon with peaks at m/z 28 and 30 and the peak at m/z 29 left out, with an answer key under the graph
caption: The mass spectrum of silicon with its peak at m/z 29 left out, for students to draw in. The peaks at m/z 28 (92.22%) and 30 (3.09%) are shown, so the missing isotope’s abundance is what’s left of 100%. The answer key names the missing peak and gives silicon’s relative atomic mass.

title: Identify the element from its mass spectrum
description: An unnamed element’s mass spectrum with two nearly equal peaks at m/z 79 and 81, labeled 50.69% and 49.31%
caption: The mass spectrum of an unnamed element, for students to identify: two nearly equal peaks at m/z 79 and 81, labeled with their percent abundances. The weighted average mass is about 79.9, which is bromine.

title: Mass spectrum of a made-up element
description: The mass spectrum of Element Q: a peak at m/z 20 labeled 90% and a peak at m/z 22 labeled 10%, with an answer key under the graph
caption: The mass spectrum of a made-up Element Q with two isotopes typed in by the teacher: mass 20 at 90% and mass 22 at 10%, so students can’t look the answer up. They work out its relative atomic mass, 20 × 0.90 + 22 × 0.10, which the answer key under the graph gives.

title: Mass spectrum of chlorine with its relative atomic mass
description: The mass spectrum of chlorine: a peak at m/z 35 labeled 75.76% and a peak at m/z 37 labeled 24.24%, with an answer key under the graph
caption: The mass spectrum of chlorine, with peaks at m/z 35 and 37 for its two isotopes, chlorine-35 at 75.76% and chlorine-37 at 24.24%, about three to one. The answer key under the graph gives chlorine’s relative atomic mass, the average of the two isotopes’ masses weighted by their abundances.

title: Mass spectrum of magnesium
description: The mass spectrum of magnesium: three peaks at m/z 24, 25 and 26 labeled 78.99%, 10.00% and 11.01%
caption: The mass spectrum of magnesium: one peak for each of its three natural isotopes, at m/z 24, 25 and 26, each as tall as its percent abundance and labeled with it. Magnesium-24 makes up nearly four fifths of natural magnesium, which is why its relative atomic mass is close to 24.

title: Mass spectrum of zirconium, relative abundance
description: The mass spectrum of zirconium with five peaks from m/z 90 to 96, the tallest at m/z 90 scaled to 100
caption: The mass spectrum of zirconium, its five natural isotopes from m/z 90 to 96, drawn with the tallest peak, zirconium-90, scaled to 100 and the others against it, as many textbooks and instruments show a spectrum.

title: Alpha particle symbol (⁴₂He)
description: The symbol for an alpha particle: He with mass number 4 at the top left and 2 at the bottom left
caption: An alpha particle written as in a nuclear decay equation: the symbol He with a mass number of 4 at the top left and an atomic number of 2 at the bottom left, since an alpha particle is a helium-4 nucleus of 2 protons and 2 neutrons.

title: Beta particle symbol (⁰₋₁β)
description: The symbol for a beta particle in a serif font: the Greek letter beta with 0 at the top left and −1 at the bottom left
caption: A beta particle written with the Greek letter β, in Times New Roman: a mass number of 0 at the top left and −1 at the bottom left, the charge of the electron it is. The bottom numbers balance in a decay equation, so a nucleus that gives off a beta particle goes up one atomic number.

title: Carbon-14 nuclide symbol (¹⁴₆C)
description: The nuclide symbol for carbon-14: C with mass number 14 at the top left and atomic number 6 at the bottom left, with carbon-14 written under it
caption: The nuclide symbol for carbon-14, the isotope used in radiocarbon dating: the symbol C with its mass number, 14, at the top left and its atomic number, 6, at the bottom left, right-aligned against the symbol. Its hyphen notation, carbon-14, is written under it.

title: Chlorine-37 ion symbol (³⁷Cl⁻)
description: The symbol of the chlorine-37 ion: Cl with mass number 37 at the top left and a minus charge at the top right, with an answer key under it
caption: The isotope symbol of a chloride ion of chlorine-37: Cl with its mass number, 37, at the top left and its 1− charge, written as a minus sign, at the top right. The atomic number is left off, as many textbooks write it. The answer key under it gives the ion’s protons, neutrons and electrons.

title: Identify the element: a made-up symbol X
description: A nuclide symbol with the made-up symbol X: mass number 79, atomic number 34 and a 2− charge, with an answer key under it
caption: A nuclide symbol with the element hidden behind the letter X, for an “identify the element” question: mass number 79, atomic number 34 and a 2− charge. Students find the element with 34 protons and work out its neutrons and electrons, which the answer key under it gives.

title: Hyphen notation with the mass number blank (oxygen-18)
description: The hyphen notation oxygen- followed by a blank line for the mass number
caption: Hyphen notation for an isotope of oxygen with its mass number left as a line to write on, for students to work out from the protons and neutrons they’re given. The isotope is oxygen-18.

title: Uranium-235 with the atomic number blank
description: The nuclide symbol for uranium-235: U with mass number 235 at the top left and an empty box at the bottom left for the atomic number
caption: The nuclide symbol for uranium-235, the isotope used in nuclear reactors, with its atomic number left as an empty box at the bottom left. Students look up uranium’s atomic number, 92, and write it in.

title: Orbital diagram and electron configuration of sulfur (S)
description: Orbital diagram of sulfur from 1s to 3p with its electron configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p4 written underneath
caption: The orbital diagram of a sulfur atom, with its electron configuration, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴, written underneath. In 3p, one orbital holds a pair and two hold one electron each, so sulfur has two unpaired electrons.

title: Find the mistake: orbital diagram breaking Hund’s rule (nitrogen)
description: Orbital diagram of nitrogen drawn wrong: the 2p sublevel has a pair of arrows in one box, one arrow in the next and an empty third box
caption: A deliberately wrong orbital diagram of nitrogen for a “find the mistake” question. Its 2p sublevel has a pair in the first orbital, one electron in the second and none in the third, which breaks Hund’s rule: in the ground state, 1s² 2s² 2p³, each 2p orbital holds one electron.

title: Orbital diagram of chromium (an exception)
description: Orbital diagram of chromium with an argon core: 4s has one up arrow and all five 3d boxes have one up arrow
caption: The orbital diagram of chromium, an exception to the filling order: [Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵ rather than 4s² 3d⁴. The argon noble gas core is written instead of drawn, then 4s holds one electron and each of the five 3d orbitals holds one, a half-filled d sublevel.

title: Orbital diagram of the Fe³⁺ ion
description: Orbital diagram of Fe3+ with an argon core: an empty 4s box and five 3d boxes each with one up arrow
caption: The orbital diagram of the iron(III) ion, Fe³⁺: [Ar] 3d⁵. Iron loses its two 4s electrons first and then one 3d electron, so 4s is drawn empty and each of the five 3d orbitals holds one electron.

title: Orbital diagram of iron (Fe)
description: Orbital diagram of iron with boxes from 1s to 3d: 3d has one pair and four single up arrows
caption: The full orbital diagram of an iron atom, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d⁶, with the sublevels in filling order. Every sublevel is full except 3d, where one orbital holds a pair and the other four hold one electron each, giving iron four unpaired electrons.

title: Orbital diagram of oxygen (O)
description: Orbital diagram of oxygen: 1s and 2s boxes each with a pair of arrows, and three 2p boxes with one pair and two single up arrows
caption: The orbital diagram of an oxygen atom, 1s² 2s² 2p⁴, with each electron an arrow in a box. The 1s and 2s orbitals each hold a pair; in 2p, one orbital holds a pair and the other two hold one electron each, following Hund’s rule.

title: Particle diagram before and after a reaction (hydrogen and oxygen)
description: Two boxes with an arrow between: before, pairs of small white atoms and pairs of gray atoms; after, bent molecules of one gray and two white atoms and one pair of gray atoms left over, with a key naming H₂, O₂ and H₂O
caption: Two boxes joined by an arrow show a reaction at the particle level. Before: four H₂ molecules (pairs of small white atoms) and three O₂ molecules (pairs of gray atoms). After: four H₂O molecules and one O₂ molecule left over. Every atom before is still there after, so mass is conserved, and O₂ is in excess: H₂ is the limiting reactant.

title: Particle diagram of an interstitial alloy (steel)
description: A lattice of large gray iron atoms with small black carbon atoms in some of the gaps, with a key
caption: A lattice of large gray atoms, labeled iron in the key, with six small black carbon atoms sitting in the gaps between them. This is an interstitial alloy like steel: the small atoms fit between the metal atoms rather than replacing them.

title: Particle diagram of an ionic solid (NaCl lattice)
description: A lattice of alternating large light gray negative ions and small dark gray positive ions, with a key naming them Cl⁻ and Na⁺
caption: A square lattice of 4 rows and 6 columns in which large light gray negative ions alternate with small dark gray positive ions, as in solid sodium chloride. The key beside it names them Cl⁻ and Na⁺ ions. Each ion is surrounded by ions of the opposite charge.

title: Particle diagram with a key of each atom (H₂O and CO₂)
description: A box of bent molecules of one gray and two white atoms and linear molecules of one black and two gray atoms, with a key listing a gray O atom, a white H atom and a black C atom
caption: A box of four bent molecules, each a gray atom with two small white atoms, and four linear molecules, each a black atom between two gray atoms. The key lists each atom on its own rather than each molecule: gray is O, white is H and black is C, with O listed once though it is in both. Students can write the formulas H₂O and CO₂ from the box.

title: Particle diagram of a mixture of an element and a compound
description: A box with linear molecules of one black atom between two light gray atoms, mixed with diatomic molecules of two light gray atoms
caption: A box of two kinds of molecule scattered together: four linear molecules, each a black atom between two light gray atoms (like CO₂), and four diatomic molecules of two light gray atoms (like O₂). The diatomic molecules are an element and the linear ones a compound, so the box is a mixture of an element and a compound.

title: Particle diagram of a mixture of two elements
description: A box of scattered particles: single large dark gray atoms mixed with pairs of small white atoms joined as diatomic molecules
caption: A box of particles scattered at random: five single large dark gray atoms and five diatomic molecules, each two small white atoms joined together. Each kind is made of only one type of atom, so each is an element, and the box is a mixture of two elements (like neon and hydrogen gas).

title: Particle diagram of a pure compound (water molecules)
description: A box of eight bent molecules, each a large gray atom with two small white atoms, like water
caption: A box of eight identical bent molecules, each one large gray atom joined to two small white atoms, drawn like H₂O. Every particle is the same molecule made of two kinds of atom, so the box shows a pure compound.

title: Particle diagram of a pure element (diatomic molecules)
